title: Massage for rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

items.ai_reason: The title explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
The background describes postoperative rehabilitation problems, inconsistent massage trial findings, and the absence of previous systematic reviews addressing this question.
The review explicitly aims to evaluate massage effectiveness for rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty.
PICOS eligibility criteria and explicit exclusions are provided. Syntheses are organized by outcome and postoperative assessment time, with hospital-stay subgrouping by country.
Five databases are named, and the search period is reported as inception through May 2024 for all databases.
Only example search terms are provided. Full database-specific strategies are referenced in Supplementary Table S1, whose contents are not included in the supplied text.
Two named reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts against eligibility criteria, resolving disagreements through discussion or a third reviewer.
The abstract specifies independent extraction by two researchers. The methods describe extracted information and resolution of extraction disagreements through discussion or third-party adjudication.
The main outcome domains are identifiable, but their definitions and whether all eligible measures, time points, and analyses were sought are not specified. Rules for selecting results are absent.
The extraction list includes study, participant, and intervention characteristics, but assumptions concerning missing or unclear information are not described.
The Cochrane tool, seven domains, and judgment categories are described, but the number of risk-of-bias assessors and whether they worked independently are not reported.
Continuous outcomes are analyzed using MD or SMD with 95% confidence intervals; the results identify MD as the measure for each pooled outcome.
The synthesis sections identify eligible studies according to reported outcomes and postoperative time points. Hospital-stay studies are further grouped by country.
No methods for data conversions, missing summary statistics, or other preparation for synthesis are described.
Study characteristics are organized in Table 1, and outcome-specific forest plots display pooled results by postoperative time point and country subgroup.
The report names Review Manager and Stata, specifies fixed- versus random-effects selection using I² thresholds, and describes Q and I² assessments of heterogeneity.
Country-based subgroup analysis is specified to explore heterogeneity, with China compared against other countries for hospital stay.
The authors explicitly state that sensitivity analyses were not performed because too few studies contributed to each outcome.
Publication bias assessment is described using Begg’s and Egger’s tests with a significance threshold of p < 0.05.
No method or framework for assessing certainty in the body of evidence is reported.
The report traces 554 records through removal of 135 records, exclusion of 398 at initial screening, assessment of 21 full texts, and inclusion of 11 studies, with full-text exclusion categories.
Full-text exclusion reasons and counts are reported, but the excluded studies are not individually cited.
Table 1 cites all 11 included studies and presents countries, participant characteristics, sample sizes, interventions, duration, assessment times, outcomes, and adverse events.

The narrative reports selected bias-related characteristics, but complete study-level judgments are not provided in the supplied text. Detailed assessments are referenced only in the unavailable Figure 2.
The supplied text presents pooled estimates but not individual-study outcome means, variability, and effect estimates with precision. Referenced forest plots are not reproduced.
Contributing studies and participant counts are identified for syntheses, but risk of bias is not summarized separately for each synthesis.
Overall and subgroup meta-analysis results include mean differences, 95% confidence intervals, I² values, and descriptions of effect direction.
Country subgroup results for hospital stay are presented with estimates, confidence intervals, and heterogeneity values, identifying country as a possible source of heterogeneity.
No sensitivity-analysis results are presented; the authors explicitly state that these analyses were not performed.

The report identifies potential publication bias for postoperative day-14 pain, gives Egger’s p-value, reports no significant findings elsewhere, and specifies outcomes for which Egger’s test could not be performed.
The conclusion broadly labels evidence low to moderate quality, but outcome-specific certainty assessments are not presented.
The discussion interprets pain, mobility, D-dimer, and hospital-stay findings alongside existing evidence about massage mechanisms and postoperative rehabilitation.
Limitations include geographic concentration, inadequate blinding, substantial heterogeneity, missing relevant outcomes, and insufficient adverse-event detail.
The authors discuss potentially overlooked gray literature and the absence of sensitivity analyses as limitations affecting completeness and robustness.

Massage is proposed as an adjunctive rehabilitation treatment. Future research recommendations include larger multicenter trials, stronger methods, standardized massage, and improved outcome and adverse-event measurement.
PROSPERO registration is reported with identifier CRD42023411680.
The authors identify the registered review protocol in PROSPERO and provide its registration number, allowing the protocol record to be located.
No protocol or registration amendments are described, and there is no statement that no amendments occurred.
The funding and acknowledgements sections both state 'Not applicable,' indicating no reported financial or acknowledged non-financial support.
The authors explicitly declare that they have no competing interests.
Datasets are available only from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Public access locations for extracted data, analysis data, collection forms, and analytic code are not reported.
The title explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis.
The abstract explicitly states the objective: evaluating massage effectiveness for postoperative rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty.
Eligibility is specified as randomized controlled trials evaluating massage for postoperative total knee arthroplasty rehabilitation, defining eligible study design, intervention, and population.
Five databases are named, and the search period is reported as inception to May 2024.
The abstract specifies the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool.
The abstract reports meta-analysis of specified outcomes and subgroup analysis by geographical region.
The abstract reports 11 randomized controlled trials with 940 participants and identifies the intervention and postoperative rehabilitation population.
Results and effect directions are described, but no numerical summary estimates or confidence intervals are reported despite conducting a meta-analysis.
The abstract explicitly identifies substantial study heterogeneity as a limitation of the evidence.
The abstract interprets benefits for pain and knee range of motion, notes no benefit for D-dimer levels, and suggests massage as an adjunctive rehabilitation treatment.
The abstract does not report a funding source for the review.
The abstract does not provide a register name or registration number.
